subject: maths
title: Introduction to compound interest
summary: Calculate compound interest year by year and with A = P(1 + r)ⁿ, including monthly compounding, and compare it with simple interest.
body:
Most real savings accounts and loans use **compound interest**: the interest is added to your balance, and then that interest earns interest too. Over many years this "interest on interest" makes a huge difference — it is why saving early pays off, and why credit card debt can grow so fast.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can calculate compound interest year by year and with the formula A = P(1 + r)ⁿ, find the interest earned, and compare compound and simple interest.

## Before you start

You need **Simple interest** (the last lesson) and multipliers from **Percentages and money**. You may use a calculator in this lesson.

Warm-up (answers below):
1. What do you multiply by to increase an amount by 5%?
2. Work out 1.05².

Answers: 1. 100% + 5% = 105%, so **× 1.05**. 2. 1.05 × 1.05 = **1.1025**.

## Think of it like this

### A rolling snowball

Roll a small snowball across the snow and it picks up a layer of snow. Now it is bigger, so on the next roll it picks up an even bigger layer. Compound interest works the same way: each year's interest is added to the balance, so the next year's interest is worked out on a bigger amount, and the balance grows faster and faster.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a real snowball picks up snow unevenly and can break apart. Compound interest is exact — the balance is multiplied by the same number every period, and it never shrinks (unless you withdraw money).

## Key ideas

### Interest on interest

With **compound interest**, at the end of each **compounding period** (often a year or a month) the interest is added to the balance. The next interest is then a percentage of the **new** balance.

$1000 at 10% p.a., compounded annually:

| Year | Start balance | Interest (10%) | End balance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $1000 | $100 | $1100 |
| 2 | $1100 | $110 | $1210 |
| 3 | $1210 | $121 | $1331 |

The interest grows every year: $100, $110, $121, …

### The compound interest formula

Each year the balance is multiplied by (1 + r), so after n years:

**A = P(1 + r)ⁿ**

- A = final amount, P = principal,
- r = interest rate **per compounding period**, as a decimal,
- n = the **number of compounding periods**.

The interest earned is **I = A − P**.

### Compounding more often

If interest is compounded **monthly**, divide the yearly rate by 12 and multiply the number of years by 12. For 6% p.a. compounded monthly for 2 years: r = 0.06 ÷ 12 = 0.005 and n = 2 × 12 = 24.

### Compound versus simple

Simple interest adds the same amount every year (equal steps). Compound interest adds more each year, so for the same rate and time it always ends up higher — and the gap keeps widening.

![Paired column graph of $1000 at 10% p.a. from the start to year 5: simple interest balances $1000, $1100, $1200, $1300, $1400, $1500; compound interest balances $1000, $1100, $1210, $1331, $1464.10, $1610.51](/diagrams/y9/maths/introduction-to-compound-interest-compare.svg)

## Worked examples

### Example 1

$1000 is invested at 10% p.a. compounded annually. Find the balance after 3 years, year by year.

Step 1: year 1: 1000 × 1.1 = $1100 — a 10% increase is × 1.1.
Step 2: year 2: 1100 × 1.1 = $1210 — the interest is on the new balance.
Step 3: year 3: 1210 × 1.1 = **$1331**.
Check with the formula: 1000 × 1.1³ = 1000 × 1.331 = $1331 ✓

### Example 2

$5000 is invested at 4% p.a. compounded annually for 6 years. Find the final amount and the interest earned.

Step 1: P = 5000, r = 0.04, n = 6.
Step 2: A = 5000 × 1.04⁶ = 6326.595… ≈ **$6326.60** (round money to the nearest cent, at the end).
Step 3: I = A − P = 6326.60 − 5000 = **$1326.60**.

### Example 3

Compare $1000 at 10% p.a. for 5 years with simple interest and with compound interest (annually).

Step 1: simple: I = 1000 × 0.1 × 5 = $500, so A = **$1500**.
Step 2: compound: A = 1000 × 1.1⁵ = **$1610.51**.
Step 3: difference: 1610.51 − 1500 = $110.51 more with compound interest — the extra comes from interest on interest (see the graph).

### Example 4

$2000 is invested at 6% p.a. compounded monthly for 2 years. Find the final amount.

Step 1: rate per month: r = 0.06 ÷ 12 = 0.005 — the rate must match the period.
Step 2: number of months: n = 2 × 12 = 24.
Step 3: A = 2000 × 1.005²⁴ = 2254.319… ≈ **$2254.32**.

## Common mistakes

- **Using simple interest by mistake.** Compound interest is not P × r × n. Multiply by (1 + r) each period.
- **Forgetting the "1 +".** 1000 × 0.1³ = 1 is nonsense. The multiplier for 10% growth is 1.1.
- **Mixing up periods.** For monthly compounding, use the monthly rate (r ÷ 12) and the number of months.
- **Giving A when the question asks for interest.** Interest = A − P.
- **Rounding too early.** Keep the full calculator value and round to the cent at the end.

## Tips to remember

- **"Snowball, not staircase"** (a made-up memory trick): compound interest snowballs; simple interest climbs equal steps.
- **A = P(1 + r)ⁿ — "the principal times the growth multiplier, n times".**
- **Match the rate and the periods:** monthly compounding → monthly rate and number of months.
- **Interest = A − P** — always subtract the principal at the end.
- **Quick check:** compound interest should be a little more than simple interest for the same rate and time.

## Key terms

- **Compound interest** — interest that is added to the balance so that it also earns interest.
- **Compounding period** — how often interest is added: yearly, monthly, and so on.
- **Compounded annually** — interest added once a year.
- **Compounded monthly** — interest added every month, at one-twelfth of the yearly rate.
- **Growth multiplier** — 1 + r, the number the balance is multiplied by each period.

## Summary

- Compound interest earns interest on interest, so the balance grows faster each period.
- A = P(1 + r)ⁿ, with r per period as a decimal and n the number of periods.
- Interest earned = A − P.
- For monthly compounding, use r ÷ 12 and the number of months.
- For the same rate and time, compound interest beats simple interest, and the gap widens over time.

questions.prompt: What makes compound interest different from simple interest?

options.A: Interest is added to the balance and then earns interest itself
options.B: The interest is the same amount every year
options.C: The interest rate goes up every year
options.D: Interest is only paid at the very end

questions.explanation: With compound interest, each period's interest is added to the balance, so later interest is calculated on a bigger amount. Equal interest every year is simple interest.
steps: Compound interest: interest is added to the balance each period.
The next interest is worked out on the new, bigger balance — interest on interest.

mistakes.B: Step 2: that describes simple interest. Compound interest grows each year.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the rate stays the same. The interest grows because the balance it is worked out on grows.
mistakes.D: Step 1: with compound interest, interest is added at the end of every period, not just at the end.

questions.prompt: $500 is invested at 10% p.a. compounded annually. What is the balance after 2 years?
questions.explanation: Year 1: 500 × 1.1 = $550. Year 2: 550 × 1.1 = $605. $600 uses simple interest, missing the $5 interest on interest.

mistakes.A: Step 2: that is simple interest. In year 2 the 10% is on $550, so the interest is $55, not $50.
mistakes.B: Step 1: that is the balance after only 1 year. Do the second year too.
mistakes.D: Step 2: $105 is the interest earned. The question asks for the balance.

questions.prompt: An account grows at 6% p.a. compounded annually. What do you multiply the balance by each year?
questions.explanation: Growing by 6% means the new balance is 106% of the old one, which is 1.06. × 0.06 would give only the interest.
steps: The new balance is 100% + 6% = 106% of the old balance.

mistakes.A: Step 2: × 0.06 finds only the interest. To get the new balance, use 100% + 6% = 106%.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 1.6 means 160%, a 60% increase. 6% is 0.06, so the multiplier is 1.06.
mistakes.C: Step 1: change 6% to a decimal (0.06) and add it to 1.

questions.prompt: The column graph shows a compound interest account at 10% p.a. compounded annually. If the pattern continues, what will the balance be at the end of year 4?
questions.diagram_alt: Column graph of a compound interest account: start $1000, year 1 $1100, year 2 $1210, year 3 $1331
questions.explanation: Year 3 balance is $1331, and 1331 × 1.1 = $1464.10. $1431 wrongly adds a fixed $100, like simple interest.
steps: Read the graph: the year 3 balance is $1331.

mistakes.A: Step 2: adding $100 each year is simple interest. Each year the interest is 10% of the latest balance.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you added last year's interest ($121) again. The interest grows: find 10% of $1331.
mistakes.D: Step 1: that is the balance after 5 years. Do just one more year after year 3.

questions.prompt: $3000 is invested at 5% p.a. compounded annually for 3 years. Find the final amount. (You may use a calculator.)
questions.explanation: A = 3000 × 1.05³ = 3472.875 ≈ $3472.88. $3450 is the simple interest answer.

mistakes.B: Step 2: that is simple interest (3 × $150). Use A = P(1 + r)ⁿ.
mistakes.C: Step 3: $472.88 is the interest. The question asks for the final amount.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 5% = 0.05, so the multiplier is 1.05, not 1.5.

questions.prompt: $8000 is invested at 3% p.a. compounded annually for 4 years. How much interest is earned? (You may use a calculator.)
questions.explanation: A = 8000 × 1.03⁴ = 9004.07, so the interest is 9004.07 − 8000 = $1004.07. $960 is the simple interest answer.

mistakes.A: Step 2: $960 is simple interest. Use A = P(1 + r)ⁿ, then subtract P.
mistakes.B: Step 3: that is the final amount. Subtract the principal to find the interest.
mistakes.D: Step 2: $240 is the interest for the first year only.

questions.prompt: $4000 is invested at 6% p.a. compounded monthly for 1 year. Find the final amount. (You may use a calculator.)
questions.explanation: r = 0.06 ÷ 12 = 0.005 and n = 12, so A = 4000 × 1.005¹² = $4246.71. Using 6% per month gives the far-too-big $8048.79.

mistakes.A: Step 1: that is 6% added once. Monthly compounding adds 0.5% twelve times.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 6% is the yearly rate. The monthly rate is 6% ÷ 12 = 0.5%.
mistakes.C: Step 2: that is only one month. There are 12 compounding periods in a year.

questions.prompt: Account A pays 5% p.a. simple interest. Account B pays 4.8% p.a. compounded annually. $10 000 is invested for 10 years. Which gives the bigger final amount, and by how much? (You may use a calculator.)

options.A: Account A, because its rate is higher

questions.explanation: A: 10 000 + 10 000 × 0.05 × 10 = $15 000. B: 10 000 × 1.048¹⁰ = $15 981.33. B is $981.33 more. Comparing the rates alone ignores compounding.
steps: Difference: 15 981.33 − 15 000 = $981.33, so Account B is bigger.

mistakes.A: Step 2: work out both amounts. Over 10 years, interest on interest beats a slightly higher simple rate.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you treated both accounts as simple interest. Account B compounds: use 10 000 × 1.048¹⁰.
mistakes.D: Step 3: $15 981.33 is Account B's final amount. Subtract Account A's amount.

questions.prompt: $2000 is invested at 7% p.a. compounded annually. After how many whole years will the balance first be more than $2800? (You may use a calculator.)
questions.explanation: 2000 × 1.07⁴ = $2621.59 (not enough) and 2000 × 1.07⁵ = $2805.10 (more than $2800), so 5 years. 6 years comes from simple interest.
steps: Try values of n in A = 2000 × 1.07ⁿ.

mistakes.B: Step 1: with simple interest it would take 6 years ($140 a year). Compound interest grows faster — use 2000 × 1.07ⁿ.
mistakes.C: Step 2: after 4 years the balance is $2621.59, which is still less than $2800.
mistakes.D: Step 1: that uses simple interest (800 ÷ 140). Also, the question asks for whole years.

questions.prompt: Money is invested at 9% p.a. compounded annually. After how many whole years will it first be at least double the starting amount? (You may use a calculator.)
questions.explanation: You need 1.09ⁿ to reach 2: 1.09⁸ = 1.993 (just short) and 1.09⁹ = 2.172, so 9 years. 8 years is very close but not yet double.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 1.09⁸ = 1.9926…, which is just under 2 — not yet doubled.
mistakes.B: Step 1: that uses simple interest (1 ÷ 0.09 = 11.1, so 12 whole years). Compound interest is faster.
mistakes.D: Step 1: doubling means the balance is 2 × P, so the interest equals P, not 2P.

questions.prompt: $5000 is invested at 6% p.a. for 2 years. Compare compounding annually with compounding monthly. Which is better, and by how much? (You may use a calculator.)
questions.explanation: Annually: 5000 × 1.06² = $5618. Monthly: 5000 × 1.005²⁴ = $5635.80. Monthly earns $17.80 more because interest starts earning interest sooner.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 5000 × 1.06² = $5618 but 5000 × 1.005²⁴ = $5635.80. Compounding more often adds interest on interest sooner.
mistakes.B: Step 3: monthly gives $5635.80, which is more than $5618. Check which is bigger.
mistakes.C: Step 3: $635.80 is the monthly account's interest. Subtract the annual account's amount, $5618.

questions.prompt: An amount was invested at 5% p.a. compounded annually. After 3 years it had grown to $11 576.25. How much was invested? (You may use a calculator.)
questions.explanation: P × 1.05³ = 11 576.25, so P = 11 576.25 ÷ 1.157625 = $10 000. Multiplying by 0.95³ does not undo 5% growth.

mistakes.A: Step 2: dividing by 1.15 undoes simple interest. Compound growth was × 1.05 three times, so divide by 1.05³.
mistakes.C: Step 2: taking 5% off does not undo adding 5%. Divide by 1.05 each year instead.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you multiplied by 1.05³. To work backwards, divide.
